seo.title: Custom Automation Machines — Assembly, Test & Inspection
seo.description: Custom single-purpose automation machines designed and built in Brea, California since 2009: assembly, test, vision inspection, robotic cells, laser processing, fine wire handling and in-machine X-ray. Installed, proven out and documented with unlocked source code.

schema.name: Custom automation machine design and build

sections.title:
The machine doesn't exist yet.
That's the *whole point*.
sections.text: If you could buy it off a shelf, you would have. We design and build single-purpose machines around one part, one process, and one cycle time — assembly, test, inspection, material handling — then install them, prove them out on your floor, and train the people who run them. We have been building them since 2009.

sections.heading: Custom automation is not always the answer
sections.intro: A custom machine is a capital project. Before anyone writes a spec, it's worth being honest about whether the numbers work — so here's the test we walk customers through on the first call, including the cases where we tell people not to do it.

items: The part runs at volume and will keep running for 3+ years
The operation is repetitive, and quality varies operator to operator
You can't hire for the role, or turnover keeps resetting your training
The task is ergonomically hard, hot, or otherwise a safety exposure
Scrap or rework on this step is measurable and annoying
100% inspection is required and humans can't keep up

cards.title: Say so early

items: The product changes design every few months
Annual volume is low and unlikely to grow
The upstream process isn't stable yet — automate chaos and you get fast chaos
A fixture, a jig, or a bench-top tool solves 80% of it for 5% of the cost
The real bottleneck is somewhere else on the line

cards.footnote: If you're in this column, we'll say so. We'd rather build you a $6,000 fixture that works than a $300,000 machine you regret.

sections.heading: How a machine program runs
sections.intro: The two checkpoints that matter most are the design review and the factory acceptance test. Nothing gets built before you approve the design, and nothing ships before it runs your parts in our building.

items.label: Stage 01
items.title: Study
items.text: We look at the part, the process, and the numbers. You get a concept and an honest payback estimate before you commit.

items.label: Stage 02
items.title: Design review
items.text: 3D model, cycle time budget, safety scheme, and controls architecture — reviewed with your team before a single part is cut.

items.label: Stage 03
items.title: Build
items.text: Parts machined in house, panel built in our UL 508A shop, harnesses to IPC/WHMA-A-620, code written by our own software engineers. Progress photos, not silence.

items.label: Stage 04
items.title: FAT
items.text: The machine runs your parts on our floor, to the agreed rate, with you in the room. Punch list closed before it ships.

items.label: Stage 05
items.title: Install & SAT
items.text: Installed, commissioned, and proven out on your floor. Operator and maintenance training included, not quoted as an extra.

sections._editorNote: Describe your engineering problem, not the customer's product. The challenge and the solution are yours to publish; part geometry, product names, and process parameters are not.
sections.heading: The ones that were actually hard
sections.intro: Any shop can bolt a cylinder to a frame. These are the projects where the answer wasn't in a catalog — and they're a better description of what we do than a list of machine categories.

cards.title: Imaging inside a sealed production machine
cards.text: Part inspection required X-ray imaging inside an enclosed automated machine. The imaging was the straightforward half — containing it was not. We designed the shielding, enclosure, and fail-safe interlock system so emission stops on any access, then verified leakage at the machine exterior against the regulatory limit.

cards.title: 50 AWG across a 30,000 ft spool
cards.text: Continuous laser ablation on wire down to 50 AWG — about the diameter of a human hair. At that gauge the constraint isn't the laser, it's tension: the wire breaks under almost nothing, and a single break means restringing the entire line. Closed-loop tension control, precise motion, and regulated laser power held the process across the full spool.

cards.title: Every unit calibrated to its own spec
cards.text: Assembly and torque calibration of orthopedic modules where the target value depends on the application — a spine bolt and a knee implant are not the same specification. Each unit is assembled, calibrated to its application's torque, verified, and recorded, with the recipe selected at the HMI and results logged per serial number.

sections.heading: No black boxes
sections.text: A machine you can't maintain is a machine that becomes someone else's revenue stream. Every program ships with the full documentation set, and the PLC and HMI source code is delivered unlocked. If you want to change it yourself in three years, you can.

items.q: How do I justify this to whoever signs the check?
items.a: Usually on labor, scrap, and throughput — in that order. During the study stage we build the payback math with your real numbers: current cycle time, operators on the task, scrap rate, and the fully loaded labor cost. If the payback lands past about 24 months, that's worth knowing before you spend anything, and we'll say so.

items.q: What happens if my part design changes later?
items.a: Ask us this during design, not after. If you know a change is coming, we can build in adjustability, quick-change tooling, or extra station capacity for a fraction of what it costs to retrofit later. Machines get expensive when flexibility is added after the fact.

items.q: Who handles the safety and risk assessment?
items.a: We do, as part of the design. Guarding, light curtains, interlocks, and the safety-rated control architecture are designed in from the start and documented — not bolted on after your EHS team sees the machine for the first time.

items.q: Do you work from our concept, or start from scratch?
items.a: Either. Plenty of customers arrive with a sketch and a cycle time target, and plenty arrive with a part and a problem. We'll tell you honestly which parts of an existing concept we think will work and which we'd change.

items.q: Can you take over a machine another integrator started?
items.a: Sometimes. It depends on the state of the design, the quality of the documentation, and how far the build got. We'll look at it and give you a straight answer, including if the honest answer is that starting over is cheaper.

sections.heading: You don't need a spec to call us
sections.intro: Most machine programs start with a part and a frustration, not a requirements document. If you have any of the following, that's enough for a useful first call.

checklist.title: A description of the operation today
checklist.hint: Even a phone video of someone doing it by hand

checklist.title: The part
checklist.hint: A drawing, a 3D model, or a sample we can look at

checklist.title: Required cycle time or rate
checklist.hint: Parts per minute, or shifts you're trying to eliminate

checklist.title: Current labor on the task
checklist.hint: How many people, how many shifts

checklist.title: Budget range and target date
checklist.hint: Even a rough range keeps us from designing the wrong machine
